rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 22 compounds and locate the elution window and critical pairs. This moderate slope provides useful selectivity information without an unnecessarily long run.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the critical pairs respond to slope while bringing the last peak closer to 10 minutes. This comparison will distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs that need temperature-driven selectivity changes.

The nearly coeluting late pair barely responded to gradient slope, so test a substantial temperature change for selectivity. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature effects while retaining a short run.
Lower temperature should improve the early critical pair that worsened at 60 C. A modestly shallower gradient should improve the middle overlaps while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove low-organic time while making the gradient shallower at the same duration. This should improve slope-sensitive middle pairs and keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes; the early peaks will be checked for compression.

Use a higher starting fraction and shallower slope to improve the unresolved middle and late pairs without pushing the last peak past 10 minutes. Check whether the resulting compression of early peaks remains acceptable.

Slightly reduce the slope to improve the remaining slope-sensitive pairs, using the approximately half-minute margin before the time penalty begins. Keep starting composition and temperature fixed to measure this local tradeoff cleanly.

Test temperature selectivity within the improved gradient window, since the late near-coelution remains the dominant score loss. Holding the gradient fixed will reveal whether moderate heating separates that pair without sacrificing the early cluster.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to improve the late cluster while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. This probes whether those gains outweigh compression of the early critical pairs.

Test an intermediate starting fraction to restore early-pair separation while retaining much of the benefit of a narrowed gradient. The chosen slope should place the last peak near 10 minutes without a substantial time penalty.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 10 to improve its four unresolved pairs, using the remaining 0.6-minute margin before the time penalty. The lower starting fraction preserves more early-pair separation than the 0.30–0.35 starts.

Explore a substantially higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to test a different selectivity regime, including possible early-pair order reversals. This could improve the stubborn late cluster, although early-peak compression is a deliberate risk.

Test ending the gradient near the late cluster so those compounds finish under a constant-composition hold. This probes whether reduced gradient compression improves the persistent near-coelution enough to offset a possible increase in last-peak time.

Test a lower starting fraction with a slope chosen to bring the last peak close to 10 minutes. This may fully resolve the middle pair while preserving early separation, providing a direct competitor to the two best methods.

Reach the final composition before the late cluster elutes, unlike injection 13, to test its selectivity during an actual hold. The faster ramp should leave time for the last compound to elute without a large time penalty.

Refine near injection 7 with a slightly shallower gradient to improve the middle overlap, offsetting the extra retention with a 5 C temperature increase. This tests whether a small temperature adjustment gives a better resolution–time balance than the larger change already tried.

Use one exploratory run beyond the high-starting-composition crossover region to see whether reordered middle pairs recover separation and the shallow slope improves the late cluster. Early-peak compression is the main risk; injection 11 remains the benchmark.
Return to the best-performing region and test a slope between injections 6 and 7. This should eliminate the small time penalty of injection 7 while retaining most of its resolution gains.

Test a 5 C increase from injection 7 to remove its small time penalty while preserving more selectivity than the 40 C run. This directly checks the temperature boundary near the best-performing gradient.

Check a one-step temperature increase at the current best method, whose lower starting fraction protects the early cluster. This will establish whether modest heating improves the overall selectivity balance or confirms 25 C as the local optimum.

Test a lower starting fraction with a slope expected to put the last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether stronger middle-pair separation can outweigh the slightly poorer late-cluster resolution seen at lower starting fractions.

Test the next shallower slope near injection 7 at the preferred temperature. This measures whether improved middle- and late-pair resolution can outweigh the small expected time penalty, completing the local slope comparison.

Refine the 0.20 starting-fraction region with a slightly steeper slope than injection 14, targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes. This tests whether removing its time penalty preserves enough middle-pair resolution to challenge the best score.

Test a shallower slope at the 0.35 starting fraction to see whether the middle-pair deficits in injection 9 recover. This is a final neighboring-region check; any resolution gain must outweigh early-pair compression and a modest expected time penalty.

Use the final injection to test a shallower gradient immediately adjacent to the best method, targeting its three remaining unresolved pairs. This checks whether their combined resolution gain outweighs the expected time penalty; injection 11 remains the benchmark.
